title: hashcat
description: Hashcat is a GPU-accelerated password recovery tool supporting hundreds of hash types via OpenCL/CUDA/Metal backends, with dictionary, mask, combinator, and hybrid attack modes.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
Current stable release is **hashcat 7.1.2** (Aug 2025), which added a Metal backend for Apple GPUs alongside the existing OpenCL/CUDA/HIP backends. On Arch Linux it's packaged as `hashcat`.

## 1. Install

```bash
sudo pacman -S hashcat
```

For NVIDIA GPU acceleration you also need the proprietary driver and OpenCL runtime:

```bash
sudo pacman -S nvidia opencl-nvidia
```

For AMD:

```bash
sudo pacman -S rocm-opencl-runtime
```

## 2. Verify backends

```bash
hashcat -I
```

Lists every detected compute device (CPU and GPU) and which backend (OpenCL/CUDA/HIP) can drive it. If your GPU is missing, the runtime package above usually isn't installed correctly.

## 3. Benchmark

```bash
hashcat -b -m 0
```

Runs the built-in benchmark for hash mode `0` (raw MD5) so you can sanity-check GPU throughput before a real job.

## ⚠️ Authorization notice

Only crack hashes you own or are explicitly authorized to test. See [Legal Notes](/hashcat/legal-notes/).
Getting Started.Attack Modes:
Hashcat's `-a` flag selects the attack mode — the strategy for generating candidate passwords, independent of the hash type (`-m`).

| Mode | `-a` | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Straight | `0` | One wordlist, optionally with `-r` rules |
| Combinator | `1` | Concatenates words from two wordlists |
| Brute-force / mask | `3` | Character-set mask, e.g. `?u?l?l?l?l?d?d` |
| Hybrid wordlist+mask | `6` | Wordlist entry + appended mask |
| Hybrid mask+wordlist | `7` | Mask + appended wordlist entry |
| Association | `9` | Candidate tied to a specific hash (e.g. cracking a KeePass entry using its own username) |

## Straight mode with rules

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule
```

## Mask mode

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 3 hashes.txt ?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d
```

Mask charsets: `?l` lowercase, `?u` uppercase, `?d` digit, `?s` symbol, `?a` all printable, `?b` any byte.

## Hybrid mode

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 6 hashes.txt rockyou.txt ?d?d?d?d
```

Every wordlist word gets a 4-digit suffix tried against it — covers `password2024`-style patterns a plain wordlist misses.
Getting Started.Hash Modes:
`-m` selects the hash algorithm/format. There are 300+ modes; a few commonly needed ones:

| Mode | Hash type |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Raw MD5 |
| `100` | Raw SHA1 |
| `1000` | NTLM |
| `1800` | sha512crypt (`$6$`, modern Linux `/etc/shadow`) |
| `3200` | bcrypt |
| `1400` | Raw SHA256 |
| `22000` | WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL (modern Wi-Fi handshake format) |
| `13100` | Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 |

## Finding the right mode

```bash
hashcat --identify hashes.txt
```

Guesses likely `-m` values from the hash's structure — a good first step when you're not sure what you're looking at.

```bash
hashcat --help | grep -i bcrypt
```

Or grep the full mode list for a keyword to find the exact numeric mode.
Getting Started.Legal Notes:
Hashcat is a password-recovery and security-auditing tool. Cracking a hash you don't have explicit authorization to test — including hashes belonging to someone else's accounts, or extracted during unauthorized access — is illegal under computer-crime statutes in most jurisdictions, regardless of how the hash was obtained.

Legitimate uses include: auditing your own organization's password policy strength (with authorization), recovering a password you've forgotten for your own account/file, and authorized penetration testing engagements with signed scope.

Guides.Cracking Wifi Handshakes:
## Capture a handshake

Use a wireless tool (e.g. `airodump-ng` from the `aircrack-ng` suite) to capture a WPA handshake or PMKID, then convert it to hashcat's `.hc22000` format with `hcxpcapngtool` (from the `hcxtools` package):

```bash
sudo pacman -S hcxtools
hcxpcapngtool -o hash.hc22000 capture.pcapng
```

## Crack it

```bash
hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 hash.hc22000 rockyou.txt
```

Only attempt this against a network you own or are authorized to audit.

## Show the recovered key

```bash
hashcat -m 22000 --show hash.hc22000
```
Guides.Rule Based Attacks:
Rules mutate each wordlist candidate — the single biggest lever for cracking human-chosen passwords without an astronomically large wordlist.

## Built-in rule files

Hashcat ships several under `/usr/share/hashcat/rules/` (path may vary by distro packaging):

| Rule file | Style |
| --- | --- |
| `best64.rule` | Small, high-yield rule set — good default |
| `d3ad0ne.rule` | Larger, broader coverage |
| `rockyou-30000.rule` | Rules mined from real cracked password patterns |

```bash
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
```

## Chaining multiple rule files

```bash
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt \
  -r best64.rule -r toggles1.rule
```

Each candidate gets every combination of rules from both files applied — this multiplies keyspace quickly, so watch runtime on large wordlists.

*Part of the [Attack Modes](/hashcat/attack-modes/) page.* Hand off from John the Ripper's hash-extraction scripts straight into a hashcat GPU run.

Source: `example/john_to_hashcat.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ZIP="${1:?usage: john_to_hashcat.sh <file.zip>}"

zip2john "$ZIP" > /tmp/zip.hash
hashcat -m 13600 -a 0 /tmp/zip.hash \
  /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 13600 --show /tmp/zip.hash
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x example/john_to_hashcat.sh
./example/john_to_hashcat.sh secrets.zip
```

CLI Reference.hashcat:
## Synopsis

```
hashcat [options] hashfile [dictionary|mask|directory]
```

## Common options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-m <mode>` | Hash type (numeric mode) |
| `-a <mode>` | Attack mode (`0` straight, `3` mask, etc.) |
| `-r <file>` | Rule file for straight/hybrid modes |
| `-o <file>` | Write cracked results to file |
| `--show` | Show already-cracked hashes from the potfile |
| `--username` | Input lines include a `user:hash` prefix to strip |
| `-I` | List available compute devices |
| `-d <ids>` | Restrict to specific device IDs |
| `-w <1-4>` | Workload profile (`1`=low interference … `4`=nightmare) |
| `-b` | Run benchmark mode |
| `--identify` | Guess likely `-m` values for the given hash file |
| `--status` | Enable automatic periodic status updates |
| `--session=NAME` | Name the session for later `--restore` |
| `--restore` | Resume the named/last interrupted session |

Full option list: `hashcat --help`, or [hashcat.net/wiki](https://hashcat.net/wiki/) for the maintained reference.

Project.FAQ:
### `No devices found/left` at startup

Usually a missing or mismatched OpenCL/CUDA runtime. Run `hashcat -I` to see what's detected; if nothing appears, (re)install the vendor runtime package (`opencl-nvidia` or `rocm-opencl-runtime` on Arch) and confirm `clinfo` also sees the device.

### Cracking speed is much lower than expected benchmarks

Check the workload profile (`-w`) — the default is conservative to keep the desktop responsive. `-w 3` or `-w 4` push GPU utilization much higher at the cost of desktop responsiveness during the run.

### `Exhausted` with no crack, but I'm sure the password is in my wordlist

Check for encoding issues (the wordlist might not be UTF-8, or the hash expects a different encoding via `--encoding-from`), or confirm the correct `-m` mode — a wrong-but-similar mode number silently produces zero matches instead of an error.
